facts.statement: Istiodactylus lived during the Early Cretaceous period, approximately 120 million years ago.
facts.quote: Istiodactylus is a genus of pterosaur that lived during the Early Cretaceous period, about 120 million years ago.

facts.statement: The first fossil of Istiodactylus was discovered on the Isle of Wight, England, in 1887.
facts.quote: The first fossil was discovered on the English Isle of Wight in 1887

facts.statement: In 1901, a specimen became the holotype for the new species O. latidens.
facts.quote: in 1901 became the holotype specimen of a new species, O. latidens

facts.statement: The species O. latidens was moved to the genus Istiodactylus in 2001.
facts.quote: This species was moved to its own genus, Istiodactylus, in 2001

facts.statement: Additional specimens of Istiodactylus were described in 1913.

facts.statement: In 2006, a species from China named I. sinensis was assigned to the genus Istiodactylus.
facts.quote: In 2006, a species from China, I. sinensis, was assigned to Istiodactylus

facts.statement: Istiodactylus was a large pterosaur with an estimated wingspan ranging from 4.3 to 5 meters.
facts.quote: Istiodactylus was a large pterosaur; estimates of its wingspan range from 4.3 to 5 m.

facts.statement: The skull of Istiodactylus was approximately 45 cm long and relatively short and broad compared to other pterosaurs.
facts.quote: Its skull was about 45 cm long, and was relatively short and broad for a pterosaur.

facts.statement: The snout of Istiodactylus was low and blunt, featuring a semicircle of 48 teeth.
facts.quote: The front of the snout was low and blunt, and bore a semicircle of 48 teeth.

facts.statement: The triangular teeth of Istiodactylus were closely spaced and interlocked, forming a razor-edged outline.
facts.quote: The triangular teeth were closely spaced, interlocked, and formed a "razor-edged" outline.

facts.statement: The lower jaw of Istiodactylus possessed a tooth-like projection that occluded with the upper teeth.
facts.quote: The lower jaw also had a tooth-like projection that occluded with the teeth.

facts.statement: Istiodactylus had very large forelimbs with a long wing-finger and very short hindlimbs.
facts.quote: It had very large forelimbs, with a wing-membrane distended by a long wing-finger, but the hindlimbs were very short.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that Istiodactylus was a scavenger that used its teeth to cut morsels from large carcasses like a cookie cutter.
facts.quote: The distinctive teeth of Istiodactylus indicate that it was a scavenger that may have used its teeth to sever morsels from large carcasses in the manner of a cookie cutter.

facts.statement: It is hypothesized that the wings of Istiodactylus were adapted for soaring to find carcasses before terrestrial carnivores.
facts.quote: The wings of Istiodactylus may have been adapted for soaring, which would have helped it find carcasses before terrestrial carnivores.

facts.statement: Istiodactylus fossils are found in the Wessex and Vectis Formations, representing river and coastal environments.
facts.quote: Istiodactylus is known from the Wessex Formation and the younger Vectis Formation, which represent river and coastal environments

facts.statement: Reginald W. Hooley described two additional specimens of O. latidens in 1913.
facts.quote: In 1913, the British amateur palaeontologist Reginald W. Hooley described two more specimens of O. latidens

facts.statement: Samuel W. Williston disagreed with some of Reginald W. Hooley's conclusions regarding the anatomy and classification of the animal.
facts.quote: Samuel W. Williston subsequently reviewed Hooley's article, disagreeing with some of his conclusions about the anatomy and classification of the animal.

facts.statement: In 1993, researchers concluded that the holotype specimen of Ornithodesmus cluniculus belonged to a maniraptoran dinosaur rather than a pterosaur.
facts.quote: In 1993, the British palaeontologists Stafford C. Howse and Andrew C. Milner concluded that the holotype sacrum and only specimen of O. cluniculus did not belong to a pterosaur, but to a maniraptoran dinosaur

facts.statement: In 2001, Howse, Milner, and Martill transferred the species O. latidens to the newly established genus Istiodactylus.
facts.quote: In 2001, Howse, Milner, and David Martill moved "O." latidens to the new genus Istiodactylus

facts.statement: Additional specimens of Istiodactylus were found on the Isle of Wight, including a dentary fragment possibly from a juvenile and isolated teeth discovered via screen washing starting in 2002.
facts.quote: Additional Istiodactylus specimens were later found on the Isle of Wight, including IWCMS 2003.40, a dentary fragment that may belong to a juvenile, and isolated teeth found through screen washing from 2002 and onwards

facts.statement: New types of istiodactylids were reported from China during the early 21st century.
facts.quote: During the early 21st century, new types of istiodactylids were reported from China

facts.statement: In 2006, Andres and Ji named the second species I. sinensis from the Jiufotang Formation in China.
facts.quote: In 2006, Brian Andres and Ji Qiang named a second species of Istiodactylus, I. sinensis, from the Jiufotang Formation of China

facts.statement: I. sinensis was found to be similar to I. latidens but smaller, with a wingspan of 2.7 meters and more teeth.
facts.quote: They found it very similar to I. latidens, though much smaller, with a wingspan of 2.7 m, and more teeth

facts.statement: In 2006, Lü and colleagues concluded that I. sinensis was a junior synonym of Nurhachius ignaciobritoi.
facts.quote: In 2006, Lü Junchang and colleagues concluded that I. sinensis was a junior synonym of the istiodactylid Nurhachius ignaciobritoi from the same formation

facts.statement: In 2008, Lü and colleagues suggested that Longchengpterus zhaoi and I. sinensis might belong to the same species.
facts.quote: In 2008, Lü and colleagues instead found Longchengpterus zhaoi to be the sister species of I. sinensis, and suggested that these two may belong to the same species

facts.statement: In 2012, Mark Witton reported the rediscovery of a jaw piece belonging to specimen NHMUK R3877.
facts.quote: In 2012, the British palaeontologist Mark P. Witton reported the "rediscovery" of a jaw-piece that belonged to specimen NHMUK R3877

facts.statement: Witton concluded that I. latidens and I. sinensis did not belong in the same genus based on his updated skull reconstruction.
facts.quote: Witton's updated skull reconstruction was different enough from the skull of I. sinensis for him to conclude they did not belong in the same genus

facts.statement: It is debated whether I. sinensis belongs in the genus Liaoxipterus or is the same species as Liaoxipterus brachyognathus, given their shared formation and few differences.
facts.quote: I. sinensis may instead have been a species in the genus Liaoxipterus, or even the same species, since they were found in the same formation and had few differences

facts.statement: In 2022, Xu and colleagues stated that the differences between Liaoxipterus and Istiodactylus species were limited and required further study.
facts.quote: In 2022, the Chinese palaeontologist Yizhi Xu and colleagues stated that the difference between Liaoxipterus and both species of Istiodactylus was limited, and that their interrelationship warranted further study

facts.statement: In 2001, Howse and colleagues suggested that the missing holotype jaws of I. latidens might be specimen CAMMZ T706.
facts.quote: Howse and colleagues suggested in 2001 that the now missing holotype jaws of I. latidens may be specimen CAMMZ T706

facts.statement: In 2021, Averianov and colleagues suggested that specimen SGM 1810–01 from the Vernadsky State Geological Museum could be the missing holotype of I. latidens.
facts.quote: In 2021, the Russian palaeontologist Alexander O. Averianov and colleagues suggested that the front ends of an istiodactylid snout and mandible at the Vernadsky State Geological Museum in Moscow, specimen SGM 1810–01, could also be the missing holotype

facts.statement: It is hypothesized that the specimen entered the Russian collection when Pavlov and Pavlova visited England in 1888 and 1891, possibly acquiring it then.
facts.quote: It may have entered the Russian collection when a curator of this museum, the Russian geologist Alexey Pavlov and his wife the Ukrainian paleontologist Maria V. Pavlova, visited England in 1888 for the Geological Congress, and again in 1891, possibly acquiring the specimen then

facts.statement: Istiodactylus was a large pterosaur with an estimated wingspan between 4.3 and 5 meters.
facts.quote: Istiodactylus was quite a large pterosaur, with estimates of its wingspan ranging from 4.3 to 5 m.

facts.statement: Isolated wing-bone fragments suggest some individuals of Istiodactylus may have reached a wingspan of 8 meters.
facts.quote: Some isolated pterosaur wing-bone fragments that may belong to this genus indicate a wingspan as large as 8 m.

facts.statement: The most complete skull of Istiodactylus is estimated to be about 45 cm long based on a jaw fragment reported in 2012.
facts.quote: The most completely known skull is fragmentary but is thought to have been about 45 cm in length, based on a long-lost fragment of its jaw reported in 2012.

facts.statement: The jaws of Istiodactylus measured 28.5 cm, which is less than 80 percent of the skull length and considered short for a pterodactyloid.
facts.quote: At 28.5 cm, the jaws were less than 80 percent of the skull's length, which is short for a pterodactyloid pterosaur.

facts.statement: Istiodactylus was covered in hair-like pycnofibres and possessed extensive wing-membranes supported by a long wing-finger.
facts.quote: As a pterosaur, Istiodactylus would have been covered in hair-like pycnofibres, and had extensive wing-membranes, which were distended by a long wing-finger.

facts.statement: The skull of Istiodactylus contained very large naso-antorbital fenestrae that combined the antorbital fenestra and bony nostril.
facts.quote: Much of the skull was occupied by very large naso-antorbital fenestrae (openings which combine the antorbital fenestra and the bony nostril).

facts.statement: The orbit of Istiodactylus was reclined, slender, and capped at the front by a tuberosity.
facts.quote: The orbit (eye socket) was reclined and slender, and was capped at the front by a tuberosity.

facts.statement: A snout identified in 2021 revealed that Istiodactylus possessed a palatal ridge, a feature previously unknown in the genus.
facts.quote: The snout identified in 2021 revealed that Istiodactylus had a palatal ridge as in other pterosaurs, a feature previously unknown in this genus.

facts.statement: The forelimbs of istiodactylids were large, reaching up to 4.5 times the length of their legs.
facts.quote: The forelimbs of istiodactylids were large, up to 4.5 times longer than their legs.

facts.statement: In 1913, Hooley classified Istiodactylus latidens as most similar to Scaphognathus and Dimorphodon, considering it a modified form of Scaphognathus.
facts.quote: In 1913, Hooley found the skull and teeth of "O." latidens most similar to those of the pterosaurs Scaphognathus and Dimorphodon, and even considered it a modified form of the former.

facts.statement: In 2003, both David Unwin and Alexander W. Kellner classified Istiodactylus within Ornithocheiroidea, though the specific grouping varied between their studies.
facts.quote: In 2003, two competing schools of pterosaur classification emerged, that of David Unwin and that of Alexander W. Kellner; both found Istiodactylus to be a member of the group Ornithocheiroidea, but the exact configuration and content of this group has varied between studies.

facts.statement: In 2014, Andres and colleagues placed Istiodactylidae in the clade Lanceodontia, excluding toothless forms like Pteranodon.
facts.quote: In 2014, Brian Andres and colleagues placed Istiodactylidae in the clade Lanceodontia, which consists of the toothed ornithocheiromorphs, to the exclusion of forms like Pteranodon.

facts.statement: In 2014, Andres and colleagues established the subfamily Istiodactylinae to include I. latidens, I. sinensis, and Liaoxipterus.
facts.quote: In 2014, Andres and colleagues placed I. latidens, I. sinensis, and Liaoxipterus in a new subfamily within Istiodactylidae, which they called Istiodactylinae.

facts.statement: All known remains of istiodactylids date from the Barremian to Aptian ages of the Early Cretaceous period and are found in the Northern Hemisphere.
facts.quote: All istiodactylid remains are known from deposits in the Northern Hemisphere, dating from the Barremian–Aptian ages of the Early Cretaceous period.

facts.statement: Teeth indicate that istiodactylids were present in Spain and the UK in addition to China.
facts.quote: In addition to the istiodactylids from China, teeth indicate the presence of the group in Spain and the elsewhere in the UK.

facts.statement: The interrelationships and exact content of the family Istiodactylidae remain unclear and require reappraisal due to rapid discoveries in the 21st century.
facts.quote: Since additional members of the family Istiodactylidae were discovered only in the 21st century, with many of those discoveries occurring in quick succession, the interrelationships and exact content of the group are still unclear and need reappraisal.

facts.statement: Two North American fossils previously thought to be istiodactylids are now considered misidentified, with one likely belonging to another pterosaur group and the other to a fish.
facts.quote: Two fossils from North America formerly thought to have been similar to istiodactylids are now believed to have been misidentified; a mandible fragment from the Morrison Formation probably belongs to another pterosaur group, and Gwawinapterus is most likely a fish.

facts.statement: In 2010, Attila Ősi agreed that Istiodactylus could cut meat but noted it could not process food with precisely occluding teeth.
facts.quote: In 2010, Attila Ősi agreed that Istiodactylus was able to cut meat in this way, but added that it would not have been able to process food with precisely occluding teeth.

facts.statement: Martill agreed that Istiodactylus was likely a scavenger that used robust teeth to scrape meat from bones, noting wear-facets on tooth tips as evidence.
facts.quote: Martill agreed that Istiodactylus was most likely a scavenger that would have used its robust teeth to scrape meat from bones, as indicated by wear-facets on the tooth-tips (he proposed that scratch-marks should be looked for on dinosaur bones).

facts.statement: The fact that istiodactylid fossils are found in freshwater or brackish water deposits with terrestrial input supports the idea that they scavenged in terrestrial settings.
facts.quote: He also considered the fact that istiodactylid fossils are mainly found in sedimentary deposits that represent freshwater or brackish water, which received much terrestrial input, evidence that supports the idea of them scavenging in terrestrial settings.

facts.statement: Witton found that the feet of istiodactylids were too small relative to their body size to be used for climbing or suspension.
facts.quote: He also found the feet too small in relation to their body size to have been used for climbing or suspension, as had previously been suggested.

facts.statement: Istiodactylus lived during the Early Cretaceous, approximately 120 million years ago.
facts.quote: These formations date from the Barremian to the lower Aptian ages of the Early Cretaceous, about 120 million years ago.

facts.statement: The mean temperature in southern England during the Early Cretaceous was between 20 and 25 degrees Celsius.
facts.quote: During the Early Cretaceous, southern England would have had a mean temperature in the range of 20 to 25 C.

facts.statement: The vegetation in the Wessex Formation included savannah- or chaparral-like plants such as Caytoniales, cycads, ginkgos, conifers, and angiosperms.
facts.quote: The vegetation of the Wessex Formation was savannah- or chaparral-like, and included Caytoniales, cycads, ginkgos, conifers, and angiosperms.

facts.statement: In 1887, Harry Govier Seeley named fossil pelvis remains from the Isle of Wight as Ornithodesmus cluniculus, believing them to be from a bird.
facts.quote: En 1887 Harry Govier Seeley nombró los restos de una pelvis fósil descubierta en la Isla de Wight, Ornithodesmus cluniculus, pensando que era de un ave.

facts.statement: In 1913, Reginald Walter Hooley named the species Ornithodesmus latidens for material confirmed to be from a pterosaur found in the Vectis Formation.

facts.statement: The holotype for Ornithodesmus latidens was BMNH R 0176, an incomplete skeleton.
facts.quote: El holotipo fue BMNH R 0176, un esqueleto parcial.

facts.statement: In 2001, Stafford Howse, Andrew Milner, and David Martill assigned the species to its own genus, Istiodactylus.

facts.statement: The genus name Istiodactylus is derived from the Greek words for 'sail' and 'finger', referring to the wing membrane attached to a large wing finger.

facts.statement: In 2006, a second species, I. sinensis from China, was named, with its species name referring to its discovery location.
facts.quote: En 2006 una segunda especie, I. sinensis de China, fue nombrada, y su nombre de especie se refiere a su hallazgo en China.

facts.statement: The holotype for I. sinensis is NGMC 99-07-011, an incomplete skeleton of a subadult individual.
facts.quote: Su holotipo es NGMC 99-07-011, un esqueleto parcial de un individuo subadulto.

facts.statement: Istiodactylus was a moderately large pterosaur with a skull measuring 56 centimeters in length and a wingspan likely around five meters, about half the size of the largest Pteranodon specimens.
facts.quote: Istiodactylus era un pterosaurio moderadamente grande; su cráneo medía 56 centímetros de largo, y su envergadura estaba probablemente en el rango de los cinco metros, cerca de la mitad de grande que los mayores ejemplares de Pteranodon.

facts.statement: Due to its rounded and flattened beak shape, Istiodactylus is sometimes called the 'duck-billed pterosaur'.

facts.statement: Unlike ducks, Istiodactylus had small sharp teeth and may have eaten fish or scavenged carrion.

facts.statement: The sharp, leaf-shaped teeth were laterally compressed as an adaptation for cutting meat and were closely interlocked at the front of the jaws.

facts.statement: A 2012 study proposed that Istiodactylus was primarily a scavenger.
